title: Find a Value in a Rotated List
statement:
A list of distinct integers was sorted ascending and then rotated: some number of items, possibly zero, were moved from the end to the front, keeping their order. [3, 11, 25, 40, 52, 67] rotated by 3 becomes [40, 52, 67, 3, 11, 25].

Given the rotated list nums and a number target, return the index of target in nums, or -1 if it is not there.

Your solution must run in O(log n) time.

examples.why: The first middle is 67. The left side 40…67 is sorted and 11 is not in its range, so the search moves right without ever needing to know where the drop is.
45 would fit between 40 and 52, but it is not there. The search must still end cleanly.
With two items, mid and lo are the same index. The one-item left side counts as sorted, so the test must be nums[lo] <= nums[mid]; with < the search goes the wrong way and returns -1.

constraints: nums is an ascending list rotated by 0 to n − 1 places
hints: Cut the rotated list at mid. Can both halves contain the drop?
At least one half, [lo..mid] or [mid..hi], is a plain sorted run. You can tell which one by comparing its two ends.

If nums[lo] <= nums[mid], the left half is sorted: target is there exactly when nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid]. Otherwise the right half is sorted: check nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi]. Keep the half that can hold target.

explain.intuition:
Plain binary search needs to know which side of mid could hold the target. In a rotated list you cannot tell from nums[mid] alone. But the drop is in at most one of the two halves, so the other half is an ordinary sorted run, and for a sorted run you can check "is target inside?" by looking at its two ends. If yes, search there; if no, target can only be in the other half. Either way half the range goes.

Which half is sorted? If nums[lo] <= nums[mid], nothing drops between them, so the left half is sorted. Otherwise the drop is on the left, which makes the right half sorted. The = matters: when lo === mid the "left half" is one item, which is sorted.
steps: Set lo = 0, hi = n − 1 (inclusive). While lo <= hi, take mid = floor((lo + hi) / 2); return it if nums[mid] === target.
If nums[lo] <= nums[mid], the left half is sorted. If nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid], set hi = mid − 1; otherwise lo = mid + 1.
Otherwise the right half is sorted. If nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi], set lo = mid + 1; otherwise hi = mid − 1.
pitfalls: Testing nums[lo] < nums[mid] instead of <=. With two items left, lo === mid; the strict test calls the left side unsorted, checks the wrong range and drops the target (third example).
Using strict comparisons on the range ends: nums[lo] < target or target < nums[hi]. The target sitting exactly at lo or hi is then sent to the wrong half.

Finding the drop with one binary search and then searching the wrong part. It works, but you must compare target with the last value to pick the part, and getting the boundaries right twice is harder than the one-pass version.

solutions.title: Walk the list
Find the drop, then search one run
solutions.idea: First binary search for the index of the smallest value. That splits the list into two sorted runs; the last value tells you which run target belongs to. Then do a normal binary search there.

solutions.title: One pass: keep the half that is sorted
solutions.idea: One of [lo..mid] and [mid..hi] is always sorted. Check whether target lies within that sorted half's ends and keep the half that can hold it.

followups: Values may repeat. Return whether target is present. What breaks when nums[lo] === nums[mid] === nums[hi]?
Why must the second solution compare target with the last value rather than the first?
